messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 52, Ajay had spent most of his adult life tending to the homes of others, sweeping floors and wiping counters in a high‑rise apartment complex that housed a diverse mix of tenants. He had grown up in a modest South Asian family in New Jersey, and the pride he felt in keeping his work clean and orderly was a core part of his identity. The day he had come to work at the unit of an elderly man with arthritis, a sudden misstep while balancing a heavy bucket of bleach on a narrow corridor caused the man to stumble. The man fell onto the floor, his head striking the edge of the counter, and Ajay watched in horror as the man's face twisted in pain. The man lay still for a moment, his eyes wide, and Ajay felt an instant, jarring awareness of how his own small slip could lead to such suffering. The event was brief—just a few seconds—yet it became a mental snapshot that he could recall in vivid detail: the clink of the bucket, the man’s gasp, the metallic taste of blood, the silence that followed. This picture would later flash before him unbidden whenever a loud clatter of a mop or the hiss of a cleaning solution entered his environment. In the weeks after the incident, Ajay began to experience intense rage whenever he tried to recall the moment. The picture in his mind was not a passive image; it was an eruption of anger directed at himself, as if the memory were a mirror holding him up to his own flaws. “I was so careless,” he would think, “I let my life slip away.” The recollection also triggered a cascade of self‑blame: he was certain that the accident had been inevitable because of the way he had been careless. He felt a sudden, deep loss of meaning in his work; the routine task of cleaning became a reminder of the harm he could cause. He started to believe that every gesture of service was now a potential threat, and he could no longer see the values of humility and compassion he once held dear as aligned with his actions. The shame he felt that night in his kitchen, hearing the clatter of a bottle, echoed across his days and turned even the most ordinary chores into a painful reminder that he had violated his own standards. The connection between the vivid memory of that moment and his spiraling negative appraisals was clear in Ajay’s own mind. Each time he pictured the elderly man’s face, the rage that rose within him amplified his sense of guilt and helplessness. He came to believe that because he had acted in a way that was contrary to his self‑image, he had doomed himself to a life of emptiness. The memory thus became the engine that pushed his negative self‑appraisal further: the anger he felt upon recalling the event was inseparable from the sense that his life had lost its purpose, from the conviction that he had violated his own values, and from the painful self‑blame that the accident was his fault. These thoughts, in turn, made it difficult for him to focus on the tasks that had once felt meaningful. Ajay’s avoidance grew gradually. He would leave early from work on days when the apartment smelled of bleach or when the sound of someone saying “be careful” rang in his ears. He stopped chatting with his coworkers, fearing that a casual remark would trigger the flashback. His relationships outside of work suffered too; he no longer attended his daughter's school play, believing that the attention of others could pull him back into the memory. He also stopped volunteering at the community center, a role that had once given him a sense of purpose. The cumulative effect was a deepening isolation and a sense that nothing he did had meaning. When Ajay finally decided to seek help, he did so after a night of waking up in a panic at 2 a.m., the memory of the elderly man's fall replaying in his mind. He was afraid of losing his job and of the possibility that his anger might flare again, perhaps even at a loved one. He hoped to regain the sense of purpose he had lost and to find a way to reconcile his self‑image with the painful reality of the accident. In therapy, he began to work through the memory, learning to observe it without the rage that had once consumed him, and to re‑connect with the values that had guided his life before the accident.
